passage.title: The Bronze Age Collapse
paras: Around 1200 to 1150 BCE, many of the great kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean fell within a few decades. The Hittite Empire in what is now Turkey disappeared. The palaces of Mycenaean Greece were burned. The trading city of Ugarit, on the coast of modern Syria, was destroyed. Egypt survived, but weakened.

These were rich, organised societies, linked by trade. Bronze, the metal that gave the age its name, was made from copper and tin that often came from far away, so every kingdom depended on the others.

Historians still debate why the collapse happened. Evidence points to several causes at once: long droughts and failed harvests, earthquakes, the breakdown of trade routes, unrest inside kingdoms, and raids by groups that Egyptian inscriptions from the reign of Ramesses III describe and that historians call the Sea Peoples.
Most historians now think it was the combination that proved fatal. Each problem made the others worse, and the systems that held society together could not cope.
In Greece, even writing was lost for centuries. The lesson for us is unsettling: order and cooperation can seem permanent, but they depend on trust, shared rules and leaders who keep them working.
